title: AMAT & Cache Performance Analysis
summary: Extending AMAT across a real multi-level hierarchy, and using it to decide where a transistor budget actually pays off.

slides.subTitle: Each level's penalty is the next level's AMAT
slides.markdown:
The single-level AMAT formula (`hit time + miss rate x miss penalty`) extends cleanly to multiple levels by recognizing that **a level's miss penalty is just the next level's AMAT**.

`AMAT_L1 = HitTime_L1 + MissRate_L1 x AMAT_L2`, and `AMAT_L2 = HitTime_L2 + MissRate_L2 x AMAT_L3`, and so on down to RAM. It's the same formula applied recursively — no new concept, just composing it level by level.

slides.subTitle: A worked three-level example
slides.markdown:
```text
HitTime: L1=1, L2=8, L3=30 cycles. RAM access = 200 cycles.
MissRate: L1=8%, L2=40% (of L1 misses), L3=20% (of L2 misses)

AMAT_L3 = HitTime_L3 + MissRate_L3 x RAM
        = 30 + 0.20 x 200 = 70 cycles

AMAT_L2 = HitTime_L2 + MissRate_L2 x AMAT_L3
        = 8 + 0.40 x 70 = 36 cycles

AMAT_L1 = HitTime_L1 + MissRate_L1 x AMAT_L2
        = 1 + 0.08 x 36 = 3.88 cycles
```

Even though 8% of accesses miss L1 and some fraction of those miss all the way to RAM (200 cycles), the overall AMAT lands under 4 cycles — most accesses are hits at L1, and misses that do occur are usually caught by L2 well before reaching RAM.

slides.subTitle: What each level's number means
slides.markdown:
**Local miss rate** = misses at this level ÷ accesses *to* this level (only requests that already missed the level above). **Global miss rate** = misses at this level ÷ total original accesses, from the top of the hierarchy.

L2's local miss rate looks alarmingly high (e.g. 40%) because it only sees accesses L1 already failed on — a harder subset. Its global miss rate is far lower, which is why L2-and-below rates are usually reported globally — local alone overstates how bad a level really is.

slides.subTitle: Bigger L1 vs bigger L2/L3 vs more associativity
slides.markdown:
| Spend on | Helps most when | AMAT risk |
|---|---|---|
| Bigger L1 | L1 capacity misses dominate | L1 hit time is timing-critical — growing it risks slowing every single access |
| Bigger L2/L3 | Working set spills past L1/L2 often | Lower risk to hit time, since these levels are already several cycles |
| More associativity | Conflict misses dominate at a given level | Extra comparator delay, usually smaller risk than growing capacity |

**How to decide:** use AMAT, not intuition — model the change's effect on both the target level's own hit time and its miss rate, then propagate through the recursive formula. A change that improves one level's miss rate but worsens its hit time can still make overall AMAT worse, which is exactly the trap in the next pitfall.

slides.subTitle: Winning hit rate, losing AMAT
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A bigger or more-associative L1 can only help, since it raises the hit rate."

**Why it's wrong:** a bigger or more-associative cache usually needs a **longer hit time** too — more SRAM to search or more ways to compare adds cycles to *every* access, hit or miss. If that outweighs the saved miss-penalty cycles, AMAT gets **worse** despite the higher hit rate.

**Correct model:** check both AMAT terms together. A change that helps miss rate while hurting hit time isn't automatically a win — compute the new AMAT.
